newsitem.title: UK: Lex sees progress in core, new investments.
newsitem.headline: Lex sees progress in core, new investments.

text.p: Britain's largest vehicle leasing company, Lex Service Plc, said on Thursday that it was increasing its market share in its core activity and making good progress in building up a range of developing businesses in car retailing and servicing that will widen its strategic base.

Commenting on the company's 1996 final results, which included a 22 percent rise in pretax profits before exceptional items, senior spokesman David Leibling told Reuters the group saw growth continuing in both core and new investment areas.
The results breakdown showed Lex making steady progress towards its target of a higher average group profit margin.

Leibling said that Lex's tactical shift to higher margin businesses had been helped by a shift last year of 39 million stg of capital from the sale of low-earning car dealerships that was injected into leasing and into a trio of "all-brand" firms.
These three new companies offer body repairs, servicing and second hand trading for cars regardless of make and age.

"They are typically high margin businesses we would expect to make between 5.0 pct and 7.0 percent return on sales, while in our car dealerships we make less than a two percent return on sales," he added. Another tactical move in the car market is to build up its Hyundai Motor brand in Britain.

This activity has been reorganised and revamped during 1996 and as sales have grown to, then stabilised above, 1.0 percent of the UK market it has turned round to a 4.4 million stg profit from 1995's full-year loss of 2.4 million.
"When the profits are coming in we think it will pay for itself," Leibling said, adding, "We've gone through the start-up phase now".
Since acquiring the Hyundai retailing business in 1993 Lex has trebled volumes and doubled its market share, he noted.
At the end of this year it expects to be asked to take up an option to buy the remaining 49.9 percent of the shares in the British Hyundai company it does not already own.
Leibling said this would only have a financial impact, saying "We manage it at the moment, and we will then be able to take 100 percent of the profit on the business."
Meanwhile, the group is content with its current structure and unlikely to be looking outside for new areas of prospective growth.

Gearing fell back to 22 percent at the year-end from 35 percent at the end of 1995, a low level that reflected both Lex's continued conservative attitude to debt and also the "hidden gearing" in its large leasing ventures, Leibling said.
These are co-owned with National Westminster Bank Plc unit Lombard.
